Just last weekend, I went to my first camp-out style festival. It was a nice respite for three days, and I suppose out here in the Netherlands, these festivals are some of the best in the world -- yet I didn't know any producers. So I listened to a number of artists, and I only really found one that spoke to me in some deeper way. I made sure I saw him perform.

What followed was one of the most exciting and dream-like experiences of my life.

When I walked up to the stage, he was playing a really nice set -- and whether it was because everyone was still resting from the looong night before, or perhaps simply because he wasn't a headliner -- but the dance floor was completely empty.

Although William Kouam Djoko seemed pretty disinterested due to the lack of enthusiasm from the distant crowd -- as they sit on the far benches, chomping down on their frites and hot dogs -- I was actually really enjoying myself. And as I was watching him mix some really danceable tracks, I noticed myself getting into a groove, so I finish my beer, and being an incredibly hot, 35 degree day (95 F), I take my shirt off to get some breeze goin', knowing I'll be needing it as the sun scorches my head and back.

So I'm dancing, really getting into the music, and I'm loving it; I have some pervasive social anxiety in certain situations, especially if I'm the center of attention, so this experience was an enlightening one all the way throughout. As I'm dancing around, conspicuously avoiding looking around the scene to see if onlookers are watching, I look up at the DJ booth, and William is now also shirtless, dancing, just enjoying playing his tracks for a single-man crowd

*Sidenote: As you fest-goers or DJ concert lovers know, a good DJ tries to feel out the vibe of the crowd, and adjust his tracks accordingly, so essentially they play to the crowd. I was the crowd. It was just him vibin' to my dancing, and me groovin' to his beats. Really amazing harmony.

So fast-forward a bit, I've been dancing for the whole 2+ hour set, in the hot rays, as a frequent flurry of fellow festers are feeding me water. So at this point, I know a good 20 people in the crowd just from dancing around and helping people get in the groove of things.

As the set winds down, William Djoko (DJ) starts speaking in Dutch and points to me. I know very minimal Dutch, but I gather that he's probably saying something about my dancing. Everyone, to my surprise, starts applauding, and I'm looking around, and it's literally the whole crowd giving me a round of applause. I'm stunned, and I look up at William and just walk on over and hop on stage.

I give him a hug and tell him 'amazing set' before he realizes I speak English, and I tell him how I got to the fest and why I was the only one at his set at the beginning, and then we get into the themes of his music, and how he expresses this dichotomy of man -- the good, and the evil -- in his productions. We get into a whole bunch of philosophy of music and all of this really personal stuff, just stuff you talk about maybe with someone you've known for a while, or in this case, someone that seemed to me to be a kindred spirit of sorts.

And so I'm up on stage for the next few sets, overlooking the crowd (which is a completely different, but equally amazing view of everything, as I really enjoy looking back at all the happy faces when I get to the front of a crowd), talking to the DJs, getting their perspectives on music, and of course enjoying all the alcohol perks that came along with it.

TL;DR -- Experienced my first camp-out music festival, conquered another corner of my social anxiety, connected with people in a way that I didn't even realize was possible, and rocked out on stage for a few hours after I met all the DJs.
